The author argues that measuring organization has long been attempted through information and entropy, and that the least-action principle—underlying all branches of physics—has already been applied to chemical systems, ecosystems, biotechnical systems, and reliability theory. The central claim is that the amount of organization is inversely proportional to the physical amount of action in a system. Because actual paths of elements are determined by least action, the measure naturally captures the state of a system without needing to explicitly include constraint states. The author derives an expression for organization and applies it to the simplest limiting case: a single free element and a single internal constraint within a closed, two-dimensional square system. Under eight stated assumptions (free particles, no dissipation, constant mass and speed, fixed endpoints at opposite corners, a non-blocking and non-interacting constraint, least-action trajectories via Hamilton's principle, and an isotropic medium), the action integral reduces to a form proportional to trajectory length. The model then compares two states of the same system that differ only in the orientation of the constraint. In the illustrative example, the first trajectory is twice as long as the second, yielding that state 2 is twice as well organized as state 1, or equivalently a 50% difference between the two organizations. The author emphasizes that this result empowers all natural and social sciences to quantify organization across systems and states. The paper explicitly notes its limitations: it is restricted to closed, nondissipative systems with one free particle and one constraint, and that extensions to open systems of n elements are planned for Parts 2 and 3. summary.title: A quantitative measure for the organization of a system, Part 1: A simple case
summary.field_subfield: Physics of complex systems / theoretical physics
summary.executive_summary: The paper proposes a universal, quantitative measure of the organization of any system, grounded in the principle of least action from physics. The author argues that measuring organization has long been attempted through information and entropy, and that the least-action principle—underlying all branches of physics—has already been applied to chemical systems, ecosystems, biotechnical systems, and reliability theory. The central claim is that the amount of organization is inversely proportional to the physical amount of action in a system. Because actual paths of elements are determined by least action, the measure naturally captures the state of a system without needing to explicitly include constraint states. The author derives an expression for organization and applies it to the simplest limiting case: a single free element and a single internal constraint within a closed, two-dimensional square system. Under eight stated assumptions (free particles, no dissipation, constant mass and speed, fixed endpoints at opposite corners, a non-blocking and non-interacting constraint, least-action trajectories via Hamilton's principle, and an isotropic medium), the action integral reduces to a form proportional to trajectory length. The model then compares two states of the same system that differ only in the orientation of the constraint. In the illustrative example, the first trajectory is twice as long as the second, yielding that state 2 is twice as well organized as state 1, or equivalently a 50% difference between the two organizations. The author emphasizes that this result empowers all natural and social sciences to quantify organization across systems and states. The paper explicitly notes its limitations: it is restricted to closed, nondissipative systems with one free particle and one constraint, and that extensions to open systems of n elements are planned for Parts 2 and 3. The significance claimed is broad: providing a quantitative measure for comparing different levels of organization within the same system and across different systems, which should facilitate the development of all natural and social sciences.

The principle of least action provides a natural measure of the state of a system.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper proposes a universal, quantitative measure of the organization of any system, grounded in the principle of least action from physics. The author argues that measuring organization has long been attempted through information and entropy, and that the least-action principle—underlying all branches of physics—has already been applied to chemical systems, ecosystems, biotechnical systems, and reliability theory. The central claim is that the amount of organization is inversely proportional to the physical amount of action in a system. Because actual paths of elements are determined by least action, the measure naturally captures the state of a system without needing to explicitly include constraint states. The author derives an expression for organization and applies it to the simplest limiting case: a single free element and a single internal constraint within a closed, two-dimensional square system. Under eight stated assumptions (free particles, no dissipation, constant mass and speed, fixed endpoints at opposite corners, a non-blocking and non-interacting constraint, least-action trajectories via Hamilton's principle, and an isotropic medium), the action integral reduces to a form proportional to trajectory length. The model then compares two states of the same system that differ only in the orientation of the constraint. In the illustrative example, the first trajectory is twice as long as the second, yielding that state 2 is twice as well organized as state 1, or equivalently a 50% difference between the two organizations. The author emphasizes that this result empowers all natural and social sciences to quantify organization across systems and states. The paper explicitly notes its limitations: it is restricted to closed, nondissipative systems with one free particle and one constraint, and that extensions to open systems of n elements are planned for Parts 2 and 3. The significance claimed is broad: providing a quantitative measure for comparing different levels of organization within the same system and across different systems, which should facilitate the development of all natural and social sciences.

Research Context
Measuring a system's organization is sought as a universal criterion across all sciences. Prior attempts have relied on information and entropy from complexity theory. The least-action principle has already been applied to several physical systems. A universal, quantitative measure of organization remains lacking.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper develops a model to quantitatively calculate the amount of organization in a general system. The central hypothesis is that organization is inversely proportional to the sum of actions of all elements. Least action is deemed the most natural measure because actual paths are determined by it. The predicted outcome is that a state with less action is better organized. The model is expected to enable comparison of organization across states and systems.

Methodological Details
The work is a theoretical derivation applied to a simple limiting case. The system is a closed system in two dimensions with one element and one internal constraint. The system boundaries are defined as a square, treated as external constraints. Constraint positions do not enter calculations because they are reflected in trajectory length. Assumption 1: elements are free particles with constant potential energy set to zero. Assumption 2: no energy dissipation, so the Lagrangian equals kinetic energy and is constant. Assumption 3: mass and speed of the element are constants. Assumption 4: start and end points are fixed at opposite corners of a square. Assumption 5: the constraint cannot block the path completely. Assumption 6: the element does not interact with the constraint. Assumption 7: the actual trajectory is the one of least action from Hamilton's Principle. Assumption 8: the medium inside the system is isotropic. The isotropic medium allows substituting the time interval with trajectory length.

Procedures And Architectures
The natural state is defined where the variation of the sum of actions is zero. The Lagrangian is defined as kinetic energy minus potential energy. The action integral is expressed as the integral of the Lagrangian over time. The constant C equals twice the kinetic energy. Average velocity is solved as trajectory length divided by time interval. The action integral reduces to a form proportional to trajectory length. Organization is set proportional to the inverse of the sum of actions. The proportionality constant is set to one for simplicity. For one element, organization equals the reciprocal of the action. Organization in each state is computed by applying the formula to each state. The difference between organizations is derived as a product over states. The illustrative example sets the first trajectory twice as long as the second. The result is that state 2 is twice as well organized as state 1. The same result is expressed as a 50% difference between the two organizations. No hardware, hyperparameters, or training procedures are reported, as this is a theoretical derivation.

Key Results
Organization is inversely proportional to the action integral of the element. The action integral reduces to a form proportional to trajectory length. Organization is therefore proportional to the reciprocal of trajectory length. In state 1, organization equals C₃ divided by l1. In state 2, organization equals C₃ divided by l2. Because l2 is less than l1, state 2 is better organized. The difference between organizations is given by the product formula. When the first trajectory is twice as long as the second, state 2 is twice as well organized. The same relationship is expressed as a 50% difference between the two organizations. The model enables direct comparison of organization between two states. A state with half the action is calculated to have double the organization. The result provides a quantitative measure for comparing different systems.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The measure rests on the principle of least action, the most fundamental principle in physics. The principle describes the actual motions of objects, making it a natural measure. The model is limited to closed, nondissipative systems with one free particle and one constraint. Extensions to open systems of n elements are planned for future parts. The result empowers all natural and social sciences to quantify organization. The measure enables comparison of organization across states and systems. Measuring organization should facilitate the development of all natural and social sciences.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model is restricted to closed, nondissipative systems, limiting broad applicability. The model is limited to one free particle and one constraint. The model assumes no energy dissipation, which excludes real dissipative systems. The model assumes constant mass and speed, excluding variable dynamics. The model assumes an isotropic medium, excluding anisotropic environments. The model assumes the element does not interact with the constraint. The model assumes the constraint cannot block the path completely. The illustration is a single limiting case, not a broad empirical validation. The paper notes limitations and applicability are stated in the list of assumptions.

Claims
The amount of organization of a system is inversely proportional to the physical amount of action in the system. The organization is proportional to the inverse of the sum of actions of all elements. For one element, organization equals the reciprocal of the action. A state with half the action is calculated to have double the organization. The model is limited to closed, nondissipative systems with one free particle and one constraint. The derivation relies on idealized assumptions that may not hold in real systems. The result empowers all natural and social sciences to quantify organization. The measure enables comparison of organization across states and systems. Measuring organization should facilitate the development of all natural and social sciences.
The principle of least action provides a natural measure of the state of a system. The measure of organization is inversely proportional to the sum of actions of all elements. The actual paths of the elements are determined by the principle of least action. The method uses the most fundamental principle in physics. The model assumes the element does not interact with the constraint. The model assumes an isotropic medium, which may not hold universally. The measure captures the state of a system without explicitly including constraint states. The result enables comparison of organization across states and systems. The measure should facilitate the development of all natural and social sciences.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The model is limited to closed, nondissipative systems with one free particle and one constraint. Extensions to open systems of n elements are planned for future parts. The paper notes limitations and applicability are stated in the list of assumptions.

Ethical Considerations
No human subjects, data, or code are involved, so no ethics approval is required.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 presents the boundaries of the closed system and defines the initial and final points of motion. Fig. 2 shows the two states of the system with a constraint and the least action path in each case.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a quantitative measure of organization inversely proportional to action. 2. The strongest evidence is the illustrative example showing state 2 is twice as well organized. 3. The future path is extending the model to open systems of n elements.
